questions.question: A particle is in a straight line motion with uniform velocity. A force is not required
questions.explanation: According to Newton’s First Law, if no net force acts on a body, it continues in its state of uniform motion (i.e. constant speed in a straight line). Therefore, no force is needed to maintain the same speed.

questions.explanation: Given: Mass m=40 gm = 40 \, {g} Velocity v=2 cm/sv = 2 \, {cm/s} (constant) Surface: frictionless Unit asked: dynes (CGS) Since velocity is constant⇒acceleration a=0{Since velocity is constant} {acceleration } a = 0 Force F=m⋅a=40⋅0=0 dynes{Force } F = m a = 40 0 = 0 \, {dynes}

questions.question: An aircraft is moving with a velocity of 300 {~ms}^{-1} . If all the forces acting on it are balanced, then
options: It still moves with the same velocity
It will be just floating at the same point in space
It will lose its velocity gradually
questions.explanation: Given: Velocity of aircraft = 300 m/s300\, {m/s} All forces acting on it are balanced Relevant concept from NCERT (Newton’s First Law):A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force. Since forces are balanced → Net external force = 0 → No acceleration → Constant velocity.

questions.question: A body of mass 2 {~kg} is sliding with a constant velocity of 4 {~m} / {s} on a frictionless horizontal table. The force required to keep the body moving with the same velocity is
questions.explanation: Since the table is frictionless and the body is already moving at a constant velocity, no force is needed to maintain that velocity (Newton’s first law). Hence the required force is 0 N.

questions.question: When a train stops suddenly, passengers in the running train feel an instant jerk in the forward direction because
options: The back of seat suddenly pushes the passengers forward
Inertia of rest stops the train and takes the body forward
Upper part of the body continues to be in the state of motion whereas the lower part of the body in contact with seat remains at rest
Nothing can be said due to insufficient data
questions.explanation: When a train stops suddenly, the lower part of the body comes to rest, but the upper part of the body continues to move forward due to inertia. So, passengers feel an instant jerk in the forward direction.

questions.question: A man getting down a running bus falls forward because
options: Due to inertia of rest, road is left behind and man reaches forward
Due to inertia of motion upper part of body continues to be in motion in forward direction while feet come to rest as soon as they touch the road
He leans forward as a matter of habit
Of the combined effect of all the three factors stated in (1), (2) and (3)
questions.explanation: While alighting from a moving bus, the feet that touch the ground come (nearly) to rest immediately, but the upper part of the body continues moving forward (inertia of motion). Hence, one tends to fall forward. Therefore, the correct choice is: “Due to inertia of motion, the upper part continues forward while the feet stop.”

questions.question: There are two bodies A \& B of same mass. Body A is at rest while body B is under going uniform motion, which is correct statements?
options: Inertia of A> inertia of B
Inertia of B> inertia of A
Inertia of A= inertia of B
Either 1^{ {st }}, 2^{ {nd }} or 3^{ {rd }} depending upon the shape of body.
questions.explanation: Inertia (in linear motion) depends on mass alone, not on whether the body is at rest or in uniform motion. Since AA and BB have the same mass, their inertias are equal regardless of one being at rest and the other in uniform motion. Hence, the correct statement is: Inertia of A = inertia of B.

questions.question: In a circus a horse rider takes a vertically jump on a moving horse, and falls back on the horse because
options: the inertia of motion is present
the length of the circus horse is large
the motion is in circular path
in reality the rider does not jump
questions.explanation: When the rider jumps vertically, both the horse and the rider already share the same horizontal velocity. While in the air, the rider retains that horizontal velocity (neglecting air resistance), so upon coming back down, they land on the same horse. This is precisely inertia of motion.

questions.question: A block is placed on a table. The force of reaction will be
questions.explanation: When a block is placed on a table, it exerts a downward force equal to its weight (mg) due to gravity. In response, the table exerts an equal and opposite force on the block (Newton's 3rd Law). This reaction force is known as the normal reaction, and it acts upward from the surface of the table.

questions.question: If pulleys shown in the diagram are smooth and massless and a_{1} and a_{2} are acceleration of blocks of mass 4 {~kg} and 8 {~kg} respectively, then
questions.explanation: A succinct way to see that the lighter block (4 kg) ends up with twice the acceleration of the heavier block (8 kg) is by tracking the single rope and its segments around the pulleys: Each time the heavier block (on the table) moves a small distance, the rope effectively shortens by that same amount on two different segments leading to the lighter block. Consequently, the lighter block’s displacement (and hence acceleration) is twice that of the heavier block. Hence, a1  =  2 a2.a_1 \;=\;2\,a_2.

questions.question: Find out the velocity of block D .
questions.explanation: A succinct “rope‐length” argument shows that the velocities of A, B, C, D add up in just the right way to force DD to move at 23 m/s upward: Label the rope segments from each block up to its respective pulley (E or F), then across the top, and so on. Because the pulleys are ideal (light, frictionless) and the rope is inextensible, the sum of all segment lengths is constant. Differentiate each segment’s length to relate the blocks’ speeds. You find that the block D’s velocity must be such that vD  =  vA  +  vB  +  vC  =  2  +  5  +  8  =  15 m/sv_D \;=\;v_A \;+\;v_B \;+\;v_C \;=\;2 \;+\;5 \;+\;8 \;=\;15\,{m/s} plus a further 8 m/s contribution via the loop over pulley F (as indicated by the geometry). Altogether, vD  =  23 m/s(upward).v_D \;=\;23\,{m/s}{(upward)}. Hence the correct answer is 23 m/s upward{23\,{m/s upward}}.

questions.question: Find the velocity of point G
questions.explanation: A sufficient way to see that GG moves up at 70 m/s70\,{m/s} (when the free end is pulled down at 10 m/s10\,{m/s}) is by counting how many segments of rope effectively support the mass or, equivalently, how many rope‐segments get shortened as AA moves down. From the figure, you can trace seven distinct segments of the rope between the top fixed support and the block at GG. Pulling the free end (at AA) downward at 10 m/s10\,{m/s} shortens each of those seven segments at 10 m/s10\,{m/s}. Because all seven shorten simultaneously, GG is pulled up at 7×10=70 m/s.710=70\,{m/s}.

questions.question: What is the acceleration of 3 {~kg} mass when acceleration of 2 {~kg} mass is 2 {~m} / {s}² as shown?
questions.explanation: To find the acceleration of the 3 kg mass, observe that: The 2 kg block is being pulled by a force of 10 N and is accelerating at 2 m/s². Both blocks are connected by a spring and placed on a frictionless surface. Since they are connected, both masses must move together (unless the spring breaks or compresses). 🔍 Step-by-step: The 2 kg block has an acceleration of 2 m/s².Since it is connected via a spring to the 3 kg block on a smooth (frictionless) surface, the system behaves like a rigid connection (with internal force through the spring). This means: The 3 kg block must also have the same acceleration of 2 m/s² (assuming the spring isn't extending infinitely).

questions.question: A block of mass m lies on wedge of mass M as shown in figure. With what minimum acceleration must the wedge be moved towards right horizontally so that block m falls freely.
questions.explanation: For the block mm to lose contact with the wedge (i.e.\ to “fall freely” and not press on the wedge), the normal force on mm must become zero. Analyzing from the noninertial frame of the wedge accelerating right at aa: The block experiences the usual weight mgmg downward, and a pseudo‐force mama to the left. These two forces must combine to produce no net force normal to the wedge if the normal is to vanish. For an incline at angle θ, the direction normal to the plane has an angle θ from the vertical. Resolving the two forces mgmg (down) and mama (left) along the normal to the plane, the condition for zero resultant normal is (mg)cos⁡θ  =  (ma)sin⁡θ.(mg) \;=\; (ma). Cancel mm and rearrange: gcos⁡θ  =  a sin⁡θ⟹a  =  g cot⁡θ.g \;=\; a\, a \;=\; g\,. Hence, the wedge must be accelerated rightward with a  =  g cot⁡θ{a \;=\; g\,} for the block to lose contact and fall freely.

questions.question: Select the incorrect statement(s) about static friction.(I) Static friction exists on its own(II) In the absence of applied force, static friction is maximum(III) Static friction is equal and opposite to the applied force upto a certain limit
questions.explanation: Let’s evaluate each statement about static friction: (I) Static friction exists on its own❌ Incorrect – Static friction does not exist on its own. It only arises in response to an applied force, preventing relative motion. (II) In the absence of applied force, static friction is maximum❌ Incorrect – In the absence of any applied force, there is no static friction. It increases only when a force is applied, up to a maximum limit. (III) Static friction is equal and opposite to the applied force up to a certain limit✅ Correct – This is a true statement. Static friction adjusts to match the applied force until it reaches its maximum value. 🔴 Incorrect statements: I and II

questions.question: Which of the following is self-adjusting force?
questions.explanation: Static friction acts when a body is at rest and opposes the initiation of motion. It adjusts its value depending on the applied force, up to a maximum limit (called limiting friction). Hence, static friction is self-adjusting. Other Options: Limiting friction: Maximum value of static friction, not adjustable once reached. Kinetic friction: Constant value when the object is sliding. Rolling friction: Constant and usually smaller than kinetic friction.

questions.question: The force required to keep a body in uniform circular motion is :-
questions.explanation: To keep a body in uniform circular motion, a real inward force is required to continuously change the direction of velocity. This force is called the centripetal force and always acts towards the center of the circle. The centrifugal force is a pseudo-force observed only in the rotating (non-inertial) frame — it is not responsible for maintaining circular motion.

questions.question: The angular acceleration of particle moving along a circular path with uniform speed:-
options: as can not be predicted from given information
questions.explanation: If a particle moves along a circular path with uniform speed, its angular velocity is constant.Hence, the angular acceleration, which is the rate of change of angular velocity, is: α=dωdt=0 = d/dt = 0 There is no change in the speed or angular speed ⇒ angular acceleration is zero.

questions.explanation: Use formula for centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion: aradial  =  v²r.a_{{radial}} \;=\;v²/r. Substituting v=8 m/sv=8\,{m/s} and r=0.40 mr=0.40\,{m}: aradial=(8)20.4=640.4=160 m/s2.a_{{radial}} = (8)²/0.4 = 64/0.4 = 160\,{m/s}². Answer: 160 m/s² .

questions.question: A car of mass m is moving on a level circular track of radius R . If _{s} represents the static friction between the road and tyres of the car, the maximum speed of the car in circular motion is given by
questions.explanation: On a flat track, the maximum frictional force is μsmg_s m g. This must supply the centripetal force m v²Rm\,{v²{R}. Hence, μs m g=m v²R⟹vmax⁡=μs R g._s\,m\,g = m\,v²/R v_{} = √(_s\,R\,g).

questions.question: A car of mass 1000 {~kg} negotiates a banked curve of radius 90 {~m} on a frictionless road. If the banking angle is 45^{} , the speed of the car is:-
questions.explanation: Using the standard frictionless‐banking formula, v  =   R g tan⁡θ,v \;=\;√(\,R\,g\, ), where R=90 mR = 90{ m}, g=10 m/s2g = 10{ m/s}², and θ=45∘ = 45^.Hence, v= 90×10×1  =  30 m/s.v = √(\,90 10 1) \;=\; 30{ m/s}. Answer: (30 m/s) Explanation: On a frictionless banked road, the normal force’s horizontal component provides the centripetal force, giving the above formula.

questions.explanation: Using the flat‐road friction formula for centripetal force, μ m g  =  m v²r⟹r  =  v²μ g.\,m\,g \;=\;m\,v²/r r \;=\;v²/\,g. Here v=12 m/s, μ=0.4, g=10 m/s2v=12\,{m/s},\,=0.4,\,g=10\,{m/s².So r=1444=36 m.r = 144/4 = 36\,{m}.

questions.question: A car is negotiating a curved road of radius R . The road is banked at an angle . The coefficient of friction between the tyres of the car and the road is _{s} . The maximum safe velocity on this road is
questions.explanation: From standard analysis of a banked road of angle θ (radius RR) with friction coefficient μs_s, the maximum safe speed is given by vmax⁡=r g (μs+tan⁡θ)1−μs tan⁡θ.v_{} = √( r\,g\,(_s + )/1 - _s\, ). questions.question: A string of length 10 {~cm} breaks if its tension exceeds 10 newton. A stone of mass 250 {~g} tied to this string, is rotated in a horizontal circle. The maximum angular velocity of rotation can be:-
questions.explanation: Given: Length of string r=10 cm=0.1 mr = 10\, {cm} = 0.1\, {m} Maximum tension T=10 NT = 10\, {N} Mass m=250 g=0.25 kgm = 250\, {g} = 0.25\, {kg} Tension provides centripetal force: T=mω²r⇒ω²=Tmr=100.25⋅0.1=100.025=400⇒ω=400=20 rad/sT = m ² r ² = T/mr = 10/0.25 0.1 = 10/0.025 = 400 = √(400) = 20\, {rad/s}

questions.question: A point mass m is suspended from a light thread of length l , fixed at O , is which in a horizontal circle at constant speed as shown. From your point of view, stationary with respect to the mass, the forces on the mass are
questions.explanation: Viewed in the (non‐inertial) frame co‐rotating with the mass (where it appears at rest), we must include the usual real forces—tension TT (along the string) and weight WW (downward)—plus a fictitious (inertial) force FF acting horizontally outward (the “centrifugal” force). These three should balance to zero in that rotating frame. Among the given diagrams, the only one that places TT along the slanted string, WW vertically downward, and the fictitious force FF radially outward (perpendicular to WW and at right angles to TT) is.
